Self-taught artist Luke McConkey is on a mission to put smiles on people's faces, and that work ethic has led him to collaborate with high-street names.

It's all too easy to be cynical. In the digital age, whole online communities seem driven by bitterness and contrarianism. Enter Luke McConkey , a welcome antidote to these attitudes. His joyful illustrations are deliberately designed to cheer up viewers, because as he argues: "Smiles are infectious; they take a small amount of effort on your part but spread like wildfire."

Luke's journey to becoming an upbeat artist is built on a childhood love of drawing, spending afternoons poring over How to Draw Comics the Marvel Way before showing off what he learnt in school the next week. As with lots of creatives though, this passion was temporarily shelved in favour of more traditional subjects like IT and history.

"I still had a love for drawing, but it was a hobby which then got pushed further down the pecking order when I discovered music, video games, going out with mates and stuff like that," he tells Creative Boom. "It was, however, always there in the back of my mind."

Upon graduating from an Interactive Media Design course at LJMU, Luke landed himself a job at a design agency. Over the course of six years, he worked his way up to become a lead designer, focusing on logo design and visual identity. "Aaron Draplin was huge for me in those years around 2016."

In 2017, he took the plunge and became a freelance graphic designer, but it soon dawned on him that creative, illustrative vignettes were what he enjoyed most. As the pandemic rumbled on in 2020 through to 2021, Luke decided to pivot into being purely an illustrator.

"I started drawing and drawing, making images in different styles, and slowly got something which resembles my current illustration style, and just kept at it," he says. "I didn't want the process to get in the way; I wanted it to be muscle memory so that I could just create.

"I took a course with InkyGoodness to try and help build a portfolio and learn about the industry. This led me to realise what an illustration agent was, and in 2022 I took the punt of all punts and approached Handsome Frank to see if they'd rep me…it took a little convincing (which is a story of its own!), but they did!"

Speaking of his style, it's fair to say that joy is the common ingredient found in all of Luke's work. He puts this down to being a positive person overall. "I really like the idea of spreading joy; I think it's something you need to consciously work on," he says.

"It's very easy to succumb to being sad, angry, down, and we all love a moan, don't we? That is important, but it's hard to find good things, make people smile, or celebrate. I always like to think if my work can put a smile on someone's face, then it's a job well done."

Of course, this means Luke sometimes has to force the positive vibes, but it's a role he's more than happy to take on. "I'm also of an age where I am not really too fussed about what people think, so being a little silly, goofy, having fun and embarrassing is fine," he adds.

"If we really want to get into it, get existential, life's mad, isn't it? We're floating on a blue orb, our lives are mere specks on the cosmic landscape, and relatively no one will remember when you sang Karaoke badly in 100 years, so go, do it, have fun and don't give a fuck."

It's an admirable attitude, but how does it translate to the day-to-day grind of working life? Surprisingly well, it appears. Luke has built a varied career in illustration, thanks in no small part to always being happy and doing his best. "You don't want to be the slow, grumpy illustrator who's difficult to work with… at least I don't want to be, and you never know who's going to speak to who and ask, 'What are they like'.

"Getting your work online is probably a huge thing; I've got my website I try to keep it updated regularly. Keeping the work you want to get hired for is the main thing. Why are football clubs launching Christmas campaigns (and do John Lewis and M&S have anything to worry about?)

Chelsea, Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester City have all gone big for Christmas this year. So what have they created, and why?

When I was an eight-year-old boy, clutching my 50p ticket every Saturday to Bristol City FC's juvenile enclosure, the world was very different. Back then, a club's idea of a Christmas campaign was a team photo in Santa hats in the match programme. Well, those days seem to be long gone.

In the 2020s, big teams launch their festive campaigns in early November, around the same time as supermarkets and department stores. And just like with John Lewis and M&S, you can expect celebrity cameos, out-of-home campaigns and big-name agency credits to match.

This year, four of the Premier League's heavyweights have gone out to make a big old Christmas splash. Chelsea has built a fake TV network. Liverpool has turned its Christmas message into a thank-you note. Arsenal has hired Colin Firth. And Manchester City has handed the pens to local schoolchildren.
Let's look at each in turn, and then have a think about what this means for the culture in general.

This year, Chelsea looked at the idea of a single Christmas ad up and down, made a face, and thought: "Nah, we can do better than that". Instead, the club has turned itself into an entire festive TV network, complete with its own weather forecast, phone-in, shopping channel and ad breaks, all selling the club's Christmas range.

Sports broadcaster Jolie Sharpe sells the range, QVC-style. TalkSport presenter Jason Cundy brings radio phone-in mayhem. Striker João Pedro answers fans in Ask João, and fellow team member Cole Palmer delivers the weather "as cold as ever". Other players from across the men's and women's squads, including Levi Colwill, Katie McCabe, Ellie Carpenter and Alyssa Thompson, also get involved.

The rollout of the campaign, created by agency Till Dawn with strategy from consultancy Iconic, has been epic. Fans got the outtakes first: fourth-wall breaks, asides to camera and players corpsing. Then came the channels, scattered across different platforms, and only at the end does the full programme arrive.

"Fans watch football flicking between clips, streams, reactions and live shopping within the same phone, so this Christmas Chelsea broadcasts everywhere all at once," explains James Kirkham, founder of Iconic. "You find it in pieces, channel-hop your way through a different clip or show on every platform, and it brings back that can't-wait wanting of circling the Christmas catalogue, before it all turned into cardboard boxes on the doorstep."
"We shot it like a live network with every camera rolling, so the corpsing, the asides and the looks off to the AD are as much the show as the show," adds Till Dawn founder Craig Stronach.
A percentage of sales from the festive range goes to Chelsea Foundation and its charity partners to tackle loneliness and social isolation across London.

While Chelsea has gone all-out this Christmas, Liverpool has kept things simpler, with a single message. Rather than sell anything up front, it uses its traditional Christmas spot to thank fans, in the most Scouse way possible: "Nice one."
In the hero film, Dear Reds, players from the men's and women's teams, including Virgil van Dijk, Alexis Mac Allister, Alisson Becker, Florian Wirtz and Grace Fisk, thank supporters directly.

Their words play over photos and footage of fans from Merseyside and around the world, much of it user-generated. It ends with the line: "This club doesn't belong to us. But we're honoured to represent it. And it's an honour to play for you. To the world's greatest fans, nice one."

Out-of-home ads are appearing near Official Liverpool Supporters Club locations in 24 cities across 16 countries and five continents, from Dublin and Oslo to Bangkok, Jakarta and Cape Town. "With 'Nice One', we're putting the world's greatest fans at the heart of our Christmas campaign and delivering football's biggest-ever thank you to the people who help make this club so special," says Hannah Pym, senior vice president of marketing and digital at Liverpool FC.
This year's holiday ads have one thing in common, and it's good news for creatives
Michael Feder, founding partner at Hornet, assesses this year's batch of seasonal ads and identifies one overriding theme that unites them all. With Prada, Levi's and Dior all turning to…
Michael Feder, founding partner at Hornet, assesses this year's batch of seasonal ads and identifies one overriding theme that unites them all.

With Prada, Levi's and Dior all turning to animation for their festive spots, craft as a symbol for the holidays is stronger than ever. At the same time, convincing audiences of authentic craft is getting harder.

Dior is now facing backlash, with viewers debating how much AI played a role in creating its Marlene Dietrich-inspired spot. Director Sylvain Chomet has denied using generative AI in the project, though he has acknowledged the use of automated interpolation to generate some of the intermediate frames that make movement fluid.

It's an interesting—and welcome—development: the strength of reaction and scrutiny shows that people appreciate craft and are paying increasing attention to how content is created. They are becoming a kind of AI police, tired of shortcuts and craving care and authenticity in what brands serve up, especially when it comes to the magic of the holidays.

With discourse and changing sentiments around AI now making reactions to a holiday ad more complex, the thing that creatives can always come back to is the visible evidence that a real team made decisions and put thought, effort, and care into the final result.
1. The strongest work is built with humanity at its core.

This year’s La Mer holiday campaign shows how. Director Samuel Jerome Mason drew inspiration from mid-century stagecraft and classic holiday window displays, set in a theatrical, nostalgic CG world. Rather than simply showcasing the products, the campaign gives audiences a sense of nostalgia and artistry to admire, helping it have a human feel.
2. Restraint helps to cut through noise

The holidays are the most emotional time of year for audiences, making it an important moment to lean into sentiment and slowness. The most persuasive work has elements of restraint, particularly within the luxury industry, where quiet simplicity is emphasised. A useful test is whether the original founder or designer would recognise the work as their own. If the answer is no, it's probably too loud.

Looking to the past can help here, leaning into archival motifs or advertising. Intentional use of materials can also anchor a campaign in restraint rather than novelty, with embroidery, silk, and paper as useful symbols of luxury while maintaining craft.

Brands should focus on creating scalable worlds rather than one-off spots. The world can be used across films, stills, billboards and social assets, and be released in stages across the season. Take La Mer's 2025 campaign , which created an immersive world for products within an Art Deco, Great Gatsby-inspired party.

Similarly, the animated 'The Bear and the Hare' ad we made with Blinkink for John Lewis was accompanied by a hardback book and ebook, merchandise including toys and baby clothing, and a soundtrack by Lily Allen, which reached number one on the UK Singles Chart.

Although over 10 years old now, the world of 'The Bear and the Hare' can be revisited year after year, connected to a broader cultural conversation and emotional reaction. This makes the campaign become part of something bigger than simply a sales moment.
4. Brands need to be specific about the craft they choose

The craft alone is not the message: if every brand uses animation or celebrities to signal humanity, it diminishes the meaning. Brands should choose a format that makes sense for their category and be specific about why they chose that craft. For example, animation and luxury go hand in hand because animation shows the patience, attention to detail, and emotional response that has always been associated with luxury.

I appreciate that so many luxury brands are producing ads created by incredibly talented illustrators, animators, and individual artists this year. Rimowa's papercraft holiday campaign, created in collaboration with animation studio Studio Linguini, alongside creative agency GUT Amsterdam, stands out to me as smart and charming. Work like this promotes a sense of discovery for audiences, and an authentic connection to authorship.

Helen Bur’s Monumental Bordeaux Mural Celebrates Motherhood and Female Solidarity, France

British street artist Helen Bur has completed her largest mural to date in Bordeaux, France, transforming the towering façade of the Nerval residential building in the Grand Parc neighbourhood into a monumental portrait of motherhood, female solidarity and human connection. Entitled Matrescense , the artwork depicts two local women in the final trimester of pregnancy, brought together through a project that celebrates the importance of companionship and mutual support within the community.
Helen Bur, WIP, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The title, Matrescence , refers to the profound transition into motherhood, a developmental process encompassing the physical, psychological, emotional and social changes experienced as a woman becomes a mother. Much like adolescence, it is a period of transformation in which identity, relationships and perceptions of self evolve.

Through her portrayal of two expectant mothers, Helen Bur gives this often overlooked experience a monumental public presence, recognising not only the vulnerability and anticipation of pregnancy but also the importance of connection, understanding and mutual support during one of life’s most significant transitions.
Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Created for KIFKIF, an ambitious urban art initiative led by Bordeaux-based association EXIT, the mural marks the beginning of a wider programme connecting internationally recognised artists with local residents through public art, creative workshops and community participation.

At the heart of Matrescense are two pregnant women arranged head-to-foot, their bodies forming an intimate, almost circular composition reminiscent of the yin-yang symbol. One reclines towards the ground while the other turns upwards, their opposing positions creating a sense of balance and interdependence. Although each woman occupies her own space within the painting, their gestures and proximity suggest an unspoken relationship built upon understanding, companionship and mutual care.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Both women live in Bordeaux’s Grand Parc neighbourhood and were invited to become models for the artwork. Remarkably, they had not known one another before the project, making their connection something that developed through the creative process itself. What appears to be a longstanding bond between two women was, in fact, formed through the experience of participating in the mural.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The subject emerged from Helen Bur’s exploration of the neighbourhood’s social realities, particularly the experiences of women raising children without a partner. Rather than portraying motherhood through an idealised image of the family, she places two expectant mothers together, acknowledging the friendships, relationships and wider networks of support that can become essential throughout pregnancy and parenthood.
Matrescense: Intimacy on a Monumental Scale

Rising across the façade of the Nerval building, the 32-metre mural transforms an ordinary residential elevation into an expansive, deeply personal painting. Completed following more than two weeks on site, despite challenging weather conditions, the work represents a significant milestone in Bur’s artistic practice.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The composition is particularly striking for the contrast between its monumental scale and the intimacy of its subject. The two women appear suspended within a richly layered interior of deep terracotta, warm ochre and patterned textiles, surrounded by abundant green foliage. The arrangement creates the impression of a private domestic space opened to the city, allowing an everyday moment of connection to occupy the architecture of an entire building.

Elegance Flows Through Sheena Liam’s Embroideries in Green
Model and ballet dancer Sheena Liam brings her understanding of poise, elegance, and graceful bodily movements to a more fixed medium.

Model and ballet dancer Sheena Liam brings her understanding of poise, elegance, and graceful bodily movements to a more fixed medium. For the past several years, the artist has been stitching tender portraits of women with long, three-dimensional braids that cascade off the fabric. Occasionally, a single loose thread appears to have slipped out of its plait as it drifts across a protagonist’s cheek.

Liam’s latest works are on view this month in her solo exhibition, The Unbearable Lightness . Several pieces feature figures sporting the same striped bodysuit with an open back, and the methodical pattern on the garment evokes both a sense of precision and rhythm depicted in the scenes. Dancers grasp hands in a circle, clutch each other at the waist, and quietly stretch in solitude, their movements steady and self-determined.

Created across the last eight years, this body of work extends Liam’s interest in women’s labor and how the slow, careful process of stitching can also be an act of defiance in an increasingly digital, fast-paced world. Each piece begins with an underlying sketch that the artist then covers in thread and typically finishes with sleek braids and quick snips of the remaining loose ends.
The Unbearable Lightness opens today at Item Gallery in Paris and runs through December 19. Follow Liam’s latest on Instagram .

Andrada Trapnell: The Delicate Threshold of Vulnerability and Transformation
Andrada reveals how her art forms an emotional bridge between vulnerability and self-discovery. In this exclusive interview, we delve into the liminal spaces of self-reflection, curiosity…

There is something about Andrada Trapnell’s paintings that feels strangely familiar, as though you’ve encountered these moments somewhere before, tucked away in the recesses of your memory, only to have them suddenly return. Looking at her work is a little like reaching inside a jewelry box and pulling out a charm you haven’t seen in years. For a moment, you’re transported. A feeling rushes over you, a memory begins to take shape, and yet you’re not entirely certain where it belongs. Was it something you experienced? Something you dreamed? Or is it a moment that exists somewhere between the two, in liminal spaces?

Her paintings feel like tucked-away worlds, each one waiting to be discovered. And there’s something so intriguing about the way the recurring circles invite you to experience them. From the outside, you might take in the painting as a whole, following its colors, patterns, and abstract forms. But the circle seems to offer another way in. It becomes a portal, a threshold to something different… where the experience of looking shifts and another layer of the story begins to reveal itself.

Maybe this is part of what makes her paintings so compelling. Each one has a story. They invite you to consider the cyclical nature of life, the passage of time, and the curious ways our memories, dreams, and present moments can occupy the same space. It’s as if the mysteries of the natural world have found a home within the details of her paintings.

As Andrada explains, “I seek to distinguish the lines between dreams and reality through different styles and compositions.” A distinction that becomes increasingly difficult to make as you spend time with her work.

Her portraits, often accompanied by animals, carry a dreamlike quality, although there is nothing entirely removed from reality about them. Instead, she invites us into the beguiling abstract passages, leaving room for the subconscious to take over. A face rendered in blue might sits against a field of golden yellow, while an inverted triangle, an unexpected brushstroke, or the particular placement of light leaves you with something more to ponder.
You find yourself looking not only at the individual elements, but at the relationships between them, and what they might be telling you.

Gold leaf, intricate patterns, and layers of color and texture all have a part to play in this visual language. There is an almost delicate, spiderweb-like quality to the way these details connect, each one seemingly fragile on its own, yet serving a purpose within the larger story. Nothing feels incidental. And as those recurring circles draw your attention once again, you begin to wonder whether you’ve been looking through a window, into a memory, or perhaps somewhere much closer to a mirror.
You’ve described your work as distinguishing “the lines between dream and reality.” How do you experience this liminal space when you are creating?

When creating, I am focusing on the part of myself that draws from intuition, dreams, and the childlike curiosity for a world that has been developing and evolving within me over the years. A dream can vividly express a narrative that can bleed into your reality and make you feel that what you experience is even more than real.

Reality is full of wonder and mystery in itself, and if we slow down to take in all the aspects of life and decay that construct this circle of life that we are all embarked upon, we’ll experience a profound appreciation for the art of being, as well as the art of creation.

All of this represents an innate part of my being, which carries me through my dreams and also brings me back to the reality of life. Two realms, both with light and darkness inside. The ‘in between’ stage is the most fluid area of possibility – where two worlds merge. When creating, I am placing the subject in the ‘what if’ and ‘I wonder where’ scenario of this world.

What happens when art made for walls, rooftops and railway lines comes indoors? This November 20th, GraffitiStreet Gallery presents OUTSIDE IN, a group exhibition bringing together internationally recognised artists whose practices are rooted in graffiti and street art. Exploring the journey from public space to the studio, the exhibition considers how an artist’s distinctive visual language moves between different settings, scales and materials, and how these transitions change the way we experience their work.

A graffiti tag, a mural spanning a building, a canvas contained within a frame and a sculpture within the gallery each create a different encounter with the viewer. Site can amplify or redirect meaning, scale can alter our response, and material can reveal another dimension of an artist’s practice. Yet across these shifts, the symbols, ideas and signature styles that define each artist remain unmistakable. How much of urban art is bound to its setting, and how much travels with the artist?
As the street enters the gallery, OUTSIDE IN invites visitors to discover what changes, what intensifies and what endures.

German artist Case Maclaim , a pioneer of photorealist graffiti, moves between monumental murals and intimate studio paintings, bringing the technical precision and extraordinary attention to detail that have defined his practice into a more concentrated setting.

Spanish duo PichiAvo unite classical sculpture and graffiti, bringing ancient mythology into dialogue with contemporary urban culture. Their distinctive compositions challenge the boundaries between artistic traditions, allowing the language of the street to coexist with the enduring influence of classical art.

South African artist Faith47 , internationally recognised for her poetic large-scale murals, extends her practice into sculpture, exploring how familiar themes and imagery acquire a different physical presence through material and form.

British artist My Dog Sighs transforms overlooked objects and unconventional surfaces into emotionally resonant artworks, while Sweet Toof brings the irreverence of his unmistakable teeth motif into paintings that connect graffiti, portraiture and art history.

Belgian artist Joachim Lambrechts balances spontaneous mark-making with carefully considered compositions, while South African artist Sonny Sundancer explores the expressive possibilities of abstraction beyond his large-scale street practice. Nean Kingdom , whose distinctive imagery has become an instantly recognisable part of his artistic identity, similarly demonstrates how a visual language developed through street art can retain its character in the studio.

Although their approaches differ considerably, each artist offers a perspective on the relationship between artistic identity and environment. Moving between the street and the studio becomes more than a change of location; it creates opportunities to experiment with materials, reconsider scale and develop ideas beyond the conditions in which their practices first emerged.
An Exhibition Across Materials and Disciplines

Alongside the featured artists, OUTSIDE [IN] includes selected artworks and collectables by Banksy, STIK and TOX, bringing further dimensions to the exhibition’s exploration of graffiti and street art.

From the repetition of a graffiti tag to the intimacy of a painting, the exhibition reveals how urban art continues to evolve across disciplines while retaining its connection to the visual culture of the street.

Together, these diverse practices create an opportunity to experience familiar artistic languages in an entirely different context, encouraging visitors to look beyond the surface and consider the ideas, techniques and identities that give each artist’s work its distinctive character.

Made for the town council, the mural stops just before the first nail is driven through Christ’s hand. Brea places the moment of impending violence beside a chapel whose altar holds an image of the crucified Christ.

In Brea’s account of the composition, Christ’s hand rests against the wood of the cross while a nail is held over its palm. The action has not yet happened: the pointed nail and the waiting hand carry the tension. Brea describes the treatment as Baroque in character, a choice tied to the chapel rather than simply to the biblical subject.

The painting also draws on details at the site. Three nails represented at the top of the main altarpiece find an echo in the mural’s single poised nail and the shadow of three fingers across the painted wood, according to Brea. Outside, three granite crosses stand near the chapel. These connections give the work a particular setting: its scene begins on the exterior wall, while the crucifixion appears in the sculpture inside.

Montehermoso’s town council dates the chapel to the 16th century and describes it as regional Baroque in style. The image of the Cristo de los Remedios inside is from the 18th century. The chapel remains associated with the Feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross and devotions to Christ of the Remedies, making Brea’s subject closely bound to the building’s use as well as its decoration.

The mural is part of Vientos del Pueblo, a literary and cultural route developed with Montehermoso’s schools and local partners. The project links artistic work in the town to education and local heritage. Brea’s contribution is grounded in one place: the chapel, its crosses and the image encountered within.

Puffin: A Meeting Between Two Worlds

In Puffin , painted in Kollafjørður, a young boy wearing traditional Faroese clothing and a puffin mask offers a small sand eel to a puffin wearing a human mask. The figures face one another in an unusual exchange of identities, their shared gesture suggesting an attempt to understand the world from another’s perspective.

The painting takes inspiration from the relationship between humans and nature in the Faroe Islands, where fishing, seabirds and the surrounding waters have long shaped everyday life. Seth approaches that relationship through a reversal of familiar roles, allowing the child to assume the appearance of a bird while the puffin takes on human characteristics.

For the artist, the encounter is concerned with harmony, adaptation and empathy. Rather than portraying people and wildlife as separate inhabitants of the landscape, the exchanged masks suggest the possibility of recognising something of ourselves in another living being.

The mural’s setting reinforces that connection. Painted on a harbour building, with the waters of the fjord and surrounding mountains visible alongside it, the work occupies the environment from which its imagery is drawn. In one photograph, a young child wearing traditional Faroese dress sits beneath the painted figures, creating an unexpected relationship between the artwork and the living culture it represents.

Seth connects the painting to the migration of Faroese people who leave the islands in search of employment and opportunities elsewhere. The departing girl becomes a figure of possibility and separation, while the boy who remains watches a departure he cannot prevent.

The artist also draws upon the relationship between Peter Pan and Wendy in J. M. Barrie’s novel, introducing another interpretation concerned with the loss of innocence and the passage from childhood into adulthood. The girl’s flight carries both the excitement of discovering another world and the sadness of leaving something familiar behind.

Positioned among rocky ground, vegetation and residential buildings, the figures appear almost absorbed into their surroundings. The distance between them, emphasised by the physical break in the concrete, gives the painting a quiet emotional force that might have been lost on an uninterrupted wall.

Ted Bundy: The real reason the vile murderer represented himself in court
Ted Bundy might have the best PR in the history of true crime .

This was a murderer of women who was vile, reprehensible and violent, even when compared with other murderers of women. His crimes shook hardened law enforcement officials who covered them so badly that many of them directly led to reforms in the way that murder investigations were conducted. The way that Bundy showed zero remorse for his crimes was instrumental in refining the process of psychologically profiling serial killers. The man was as close to pure evil as you could ever get.

Yet one of the first things that anyone hears about Ted Bundy was that he was an absolute dreamboat who had an army of fans at his beck and call. One who still haunts the dark corners of the internet today.

Seriously, the man gets talked about like a real-life Hannibal Lecter. A thoroughly evil man who could glide through life undetected with his good looks, charming nature and something that gets talked about just as much as both of those, a particularly keen mind. Bundy is framed as a genius intellect who was able to get his victims under his spell, then avoid detection from the cops for years before a tiny mistake led the cops right to him.

The ultimate argument of this fact is that the serial killer represented himself in court. A decision that went so well that (so the legend goes), he nearly got himself off the hook, and even when he eventually got sentenced to death, the judge did so while saying that he was a “bright young man” who “would have made a good lawyer.” Was this actually the case? Were all these stories true, or was this something much darker?

Yeah, no. For one thing, Ted Bundy didn’t represent himself out of necessity. He hasn’t driven to do that because no-one would take his case, he was given a team of five court-appointed public defenders that Bundy quite simply thought he was smarter than. Despite the fact that Bundy was a law school dropout who wasn’t even that good a student to begin with and his team were, y’know, actual working lawyers. He pleaded with the court to be allowed to represent himself and was eventually made co-counsel with his legal team.

Which led to the absolute joke that was his actual behaviour in court. Bundy spent most of his statements in court ranting and raving about the conspiracy against him, loving the attention and supposed “control” that his position gave him over everyone assembled. He just wanted to feel important and play the role of a charming, charismatic and important man. Going so far as to ask one of his character witnesses to marry him, thanks to an obscure Florida law that a declaration of marriage in court in front of a judge constituted a legal marriage.

So, when she said “I do”, he announced to the court that they were now legally wed. Because no married man could be a bad guy, I guess. However, his true evil was still clear to see. When he was allowed to cross-examine Officer Raymond Crew, one of the police officers who discovered a victim of his, Bundy spent the entire time asking Crew to recall, in specific detail, all of the injuries made to the victim’s body. Down to the blood spatters on the wall.
He wasn’t a lawyer cross-examining a witness. He was reminiscing.

Yet, despite all that, the judge was still flattering his ego while sentencing him to death. This leads to the truth of all this. Ted Bundy was a fairly handsome, confident white man. This made people believe he was charming, charismatic and intelligent despite him clearly being a narcissistic egomaniac who raped, murdered and desecrated many women.
If that doesn’t prove just how biased in favour of men modern society is, I don’t know what could.

Despite the very concept being anathema to English culture, at least in the eyes of all the country’s most powerful institutions, porn is everywhere and pretty much always has been.

Even back when it was a literal crime to possess it, there was a thriving black market trade of pornographic images of all kinds going back so far in time we literally can’t even give an educated guess when it began. His attempts to rebuild his station ended with him accumulating over £800 of debt (equivalent to nearly £100,000 today), so he was arrested and chucked in a debtors’ prison in Fleet Street.

There, Cleland had the time to work on a manuscript he had started in the previous couple of years. Finishing a first draft and sent the first half of it to any publisher of the time who accepted open submissions. One of which was Ralph Griffiths, who was forward-thinking enough to know that the manuscript would be a massive hit despite one major problem. The novel was called Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure , and even by modern standards, it’s absolutely filthy.

The title really does say it all; the novel essentially consists of the titular character reminiscing about her sexual escapades , yet Griffiths thought he could get away with it for one simple reason. Cleland had written the entire thing without ever mentioning an erogenous zone or sex organ. Yeah, turns out the “Bad Sex in Fiction” award winners at least have historical precedent on their side because the very first attempt at getting away with explicit sex in prose still had phrases popping up like “furious battering ram” and “the nethermouth” and (I’m not making this up) “treasure bags of nature’s sweets.”

Attached was a letter explaining Cleland’s situation. Fittingly enough for a man who doesn’t quite come off as a great intellect of the time, this was a damning mistake. Cleland made it clear he was in dire straits, and so Griffiths made an offer to buy the manuscript for 20 guineas (around £6,000 in today’s money). Cleland immediately said yes, and Griffiths published the book in two halves in 1748 and 1749. It was as close to a mega hit as you could get while still being an underground concern that was highly illegal.

So, you remember how Cleland was jailed for £800 of debt? Which was worth around £100,000 of today’s money? Yeah, Griffiths walked away with a fortune of £10,000 pounds from publishing Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure , a novel that began to be popularly known as Fanny Hill after its lead character. Moondog: the street music legend of 1950s New York City
It’s a cliché to say that New York City has lost a large chunk of its soul to commerce and modernity, but as the legend that is Moondog shows, clichés are only clichés because they’re true.

In fairness, people in the city’s supposed artistic and spiritual heyday of the 1950s to the 1980s said the same. Except that to them, New York City had lost its soul because of the devastating infrastructural neglect and social decay that meant that pretty much every single alleyway outside of the really ritzy neighbourhoods (and a few in them) could be a clear and present danger. It’s difficult to argue with that, except there is something to be said for the fact that characters like Moondog will almost certainly never be found in the city again.

For 30 years, Moondog was an ever-present fixture on the corner of Sixth Avenue between 53rd and 55th Streets. Nearly every single day he could be found selling pamphlets of his poetry and playing music on custom-built instruments that were, broadly speaking, string instruments with built-in percussion instruments. You could also find him there most nights; so fierce was his desire to maintain his prime street corner that he’d often sleep there.

Which must have made for some bizarre drunken trips home for unsuspecting New Yorkers. One second you’re staggering home still buzzed from that night’s pub crawl, the next you’re tripping over the legs of a sleeping Viking.

Because yeah, Moondog had an aesthetic all of his own. One that began in the early days of his time as a busker, where he paired long robes with a shock of brown hair tumbling down his back. He then changed slightly to avoid accusations that he was pretending to be Jesus, adding Viking horns to a helmet to become something slightly less sacrilegious. One might wonder why he didn’t see the accusations coming. Which leads us to possibly the most astonishing part of his whole story.
He couldn’t see it coming because he couldn’t see it at all.

Moondog, or Louis Hardin to his friends, was doing all this while blind. This came from his childhood in his birthplace of Marysville, Kansas, when he picked up an object he found in a field that he didn’t realise was an explosive charge. It detonated in his hands, rendering him permanently blind. However, even before then, he’d established himself as a musical prodigy and, after doing some sundry studies of music theory, decided to work things out for himself, moving to New York to pursue a career as a composer in the 1930s.

After a decade, Hardin’s work was proving too out there and experimental for the classical music gatekeepers at the time, no matter how many famous fans and friends Hardin made at the time. Thus, he decided to devote his time to performing instead. That’s quite literal as well, rather than book gigs, Hardin instead took the name “Moondog” (apparently since he would howl at the moon as a child), and took to his corner of Sixth Avenue, giving his music directly to the people.

Most of the time, he avoided police attention due to the fact that he wasn’t begging. He would only accept money in exchange for a pamphlet of his poetry or, later in life, a recording of his music. He also wasn’t homeless. He’d kept the apartment on 44th Street he bought when he first moved to New York City. Most of all, he wasn’t a figure of pity. Yes, he was an eccentric, but he was also a musical genius who attracted the attention and appreciation of everyone from Leonard Bernstein, Igor Stravinsky, and Charlie Parker.

After 30 years, age finally caught up to Moondog, and his watch on Sixth Avenue finally ended. However, it ended on his own terms. By then, he’d become enough of a cult hero to be known the world over, and was invited to tour Germany. That tour was such a success that he fell for the country, upping sticks and living the rest of his life composing symphonies and occasionally touring Europe, before passing away in 1999.
All hail Moondog. May someday we see his likes again.

It Depends on How I Feel in the Morning
The director of ...And Damn He Could Play: The Marcus Belgrave Story on documentaries, micro dramas, musicals, and refusing to live in a box.

The first time I ever left the country, I went with my church youth group. We flew to the Bahamas for a youth conference, and our hotel sat right on the beach. Every morning, I woke up before everybody else. I would slip out, walk down to the water, and wait.

I had never seen anything like it. The color spreading across the water. The quiet. The warmth hitting my face before the day had a chance to get loud. It gave me a peace I couldn’t explain. It felt like I’d been missing something my whole life and didn’t know it until that moment.
I still chase that feeling. Whenever I travel, I’m up before the sun. Every sunrise feels like another shot at life. Another chance to improve, another chance to say something.
People like to ask me what kind of filmmaker I am. It’s a fair question. It’s just hard to answer.

I’ve written, directed or produced more than 18 documentaries and narrative features. One of my documentaries, about a Detroit high school, won three Emmys. I write poems. I write lyrics. I’m in the middle of creating a musical. My team and I produce vertical microdramas, the short series people watch on their phones one episode at a time. Some people are skeptical about this new format. I embraced the challenge. If that’s where people are watching, I want to be there telling them a story.
So what kind of filmmaker am I? Honestly, it depends on how I feel in the morning.
Right now, though, my heart is with Marcus Belgrave, the subject of my new documentary feature, …And Damn He Could Play: The Marcus Belgrave Story .
I didn’t come to this film as a jazz guy. I grew up in Detroit on ’90s hip hop and R&B. But the more I learned about Marcus, the more one question kept bothering me.
Why don’t more people know his name?

This man played trumpet with Ray Charles. He played in the Motown house band. He could stand on a stage next to anybody in the world and hold his own. And still, plenty of trumpet players with lesser gifts became bigger names.

The answer turned out to be the whole movie. Marcus spent his life pouring into other people. For decades, he taught young musicians in Detroit, brought them onto his bandstand, and showed them what it meant to be an artist. Regina Carter. Kenny Garrett. Geri Allen. James Carter. Robert Hurst. The list goes on. He built people, one student, one story at a time.

We spent about four years making this film, and one moment stays with me. We were in the middle of an interview with David Ritz, talking about where Marcus fits in jazz history. I stopped the interview. I pulled him off to the side, because I felt we could nail down the theme statement of the film. He understood my desire and gave an answer that surpassed my request and really shed light on why Marcus was so great.

When people talk about legacy in music, they usually mean fame. Who sold the most records. Who everybody knows. By that measure, sure, some trumpet players are bigger names. But that’s not an honest assessment. When you measure a legacy by what a person leaves behind in other people, by the careers they launched and the lives they shaped, there is no comparison. Marcus’ legacy isn’t one career. It’s generations of them.
That conversation helped me understand what was important to Marcus. It also made me realize what was important to me as an artist.

Because whatever I make on a given morning, it comes back to the same thing. I want to amplify voices that don’t get heard enough. My city. Our young people. The African diaspora. The form of expression changes, but the mission and focus don’t.

I’m a product of Detroit Public Schools. My love for filmmaking started at Communications and Media Arts High School. Today I’m one of the owners of the Collective Studios in Southfield, and we open our doors to local filmmakers who need a place to tell their stories. That matters to me as much as anything I direct.
There’s a ton of boxes out there for artists. People want to know which one you fit in so they can file you away. I understand that. But I’m not getting in one.
I can make a documentary about the box. I can make the box the villain in a thriller. I can write a song about the box, or a whole musical. I can burn the box and create art…

At the opening of “Hush Now (The Calling),” Apolonia sings to a familiar face bathed in red light, as king them to drop the mask with the gentle insistence of an old friend inviting you to sit and stay awhile. The track is the lead single from Trip , the four-track EP released November 20 by Hamburg noise-pop trio Seasurfer .

Christian Klepp ’s footage casts the first verse’s red light across the stage. Red and yellow projections sweep the back wall, while green glints in the dark glasses above a ribbed microphone. Maysterwerke cuts from this intimate close-up to wider shots, where amber haze reduces the band to little more than silhouettes.
Watch the video for Hush Now (The Calling) below.

The way the band moves in and out of view has a counterpart in the arrangements Dirk Knight began imagining in New York. “For me, this is the sound of cities,” says the instrumentalist, who recorded, produced and mixed the EP. He keeps the bass and drums fairly still while the guitars and the voices of Apolonia and Kiora drift in and out of focus.

Those guitars have been a constant since Seasurfer’s first two albums on Saint Marie Records and through collaborations with Cocteau Twins’ Robin Guthrie and producer John Fryer. This year the band put them to work on the post-punk of June’s Angels , then let them fill the room on August’s shoegaze-heavy The Noise is ours . On their third EP of 2026, a trip-hop beat gives the guitar chords more room to ring.

You can hear that space in the first bars of the opening track , One . The guitars drone and the drums take their time, leaving room for the strings that Chandeen’s Harald Löwy adds to the arrangement. The higher voices blur into the chords the way they do on My Bloody Valentine’s Loveless . The low lead comes through with the intimacy of someone speaking in confidence. It’s a seductive way to sing about making peace with your own company and the knowledge that we come and go alone.
Watch the video for One, filmed by Ahmed Sarowar and edited by Dirk Knight, below:

That intimacy carries into Hush Now (The Calling) , where a sigh of synths stretches into long, luminous lines and Knight’s guitars bring warmth up from below. Apolonia and Kiora’s voices cascade through the chorus, opening the melody out the way Elizabeth Fraser could on Cocteau Twins’ Heaven or Las Vegas and Milk & Kisses . Apolonia describes the song as a memory of first love, and Kiora hears loss and longing in the words. When the refrain comes round to “I’m by your side,” the reassurance sounds as necessary to the person giving it as it does to the one hearing it.

The guitar comes further forward on “Disappear” , where the opening loop has the woozy repetition of Cocteau Twins’ Otherness EP. The voice has Cranes’ reserve and some of Portishead’s unease. When the drums drop away, the guitar keeps circling long enough for you to stop anticipating the next hit. By the time it comes, the loop has built up a charge that carries into the closing bars.

There’s some of Cranes’ distance in the singing and some of the poise of Siobhan de Maré on Mono’s “Life in Mono.” At under three minutes, the closer rewards a second pass. Follow a guitar you barely noticed the first time through, and you can hear the arrangement shift around it.

I’ve seen Gold Cup live this year about 4 times now, and they just keep getting better and better. Despite a few technical issues at the start, they played their set as if they were the headliners. And to be honest, it won’t be long until they are headlining the Pink Room at YES. Some bands are made to be heard live, and Gold Cup are one of those bands. There’s something about their live shows that just makes you feel good and glad to be alive, y’know? I can’t wait for their debut record to come out because it’s just going to make their shows even more wild. They’re the best at what they do, and it felt like the crowd were an even split of Gold Cup and C.O.F.F.I.N fans, and you cannot help but be proud of that. The energy they have on stage and the way they play together is a thing of beauty- and yes, you will leave feeling like you want to start a band because of them.

C.O.F.F.I.N time! Where on earth do I begin? Opening the set with Out In Oslo caused the room to erupt and it pretty much stayed like that for the whole time. Part of me was watching the band, the other part was just obsessed with the crowd. It is so easy to feel unsafe at shows especially when it’s rowdy, but this felt safe. It felt like a community. And as a visibly queer person, that feeling is rare to find right now given how shit the world is. But when you find that safety net, you hold onto it. I love everything that C.O.F.F.I.N stand for, and whilst the night was ridiculously fun- they used their platform to highlight the domestic violence rates in Australia, how corrupt governments are, calling people out on their shitty behaviours and not make life harder for those of us in marginalised communities. Life is tough enough already- just be kind to each other. It’s not hard.

Every song is yelled back at the band, and there are countless stage dives and crowd surfs. You could feel the love for the band in the room, truly. And the sense of being free and being able to express yourself however you want is also felt, and that’s something we should never take for granted. You can tell that the band not only love the bones of each other but they absolutely love playing shows, and you could feel how much it meant to them. I spent the time in awe of Ben because anyone who can sing AND drum at the same time is someone to admire (within reason because there are some people who can do it but y’know…)

Every song is greeted with people in the front throwing their sweaty bodies into each other and having the time of their lives. Some of them may be feeling it today but who cares! The joy on their faces, arms around their mates and strangers- it was so lovely to see because the world is unkind, but that energy did not step foot into the room once last night. What C.O.F.F.I.N have created with their music and live shows is a safe space, and that’s something to really hold onto. For me songs like Fast Love (this was my favourite and it was a tough call) and Give Me A Bite were WILD! Think Bad absolutely ripped too as did White Dog.

You really, really felt the love for the band when they left and everyone demanded an encore (and we got it!) They’re a band that you cannot help but love, and if you’ve not seen the documentary they recently put out- please go to YouTube and find it (it may still be there hopefully.) Not only will you too fall in love with the band and all they stand for, but you’ll just be in awe of their work ethic and how dedicated they are.

C.O.F.F.I.N are for everyone, and their live shows really make you feel it, and their live shows make you appreciate the band even more. I don’t know when they’ll be back in the UK but for now, I will hold onto this show as being one of the best things I’ve seen this year.

Thoughts of dread for the living. Pandering with the queen of sorrow. Pandering to the mirrors of no tomorrow.
Thoughts of dread for the living.
Pandering with the queen of sorrow.
Pandering to the mirrors of no tomorrow.

Depression can turn a trip to the corner shop into such a long negotiation with yourself that the place ends up closing long before you’ve picked up your keys. On “Feelings Are Monsters,” Berlin’s Night Nail give that dread seven eyes and seven legs. Brandon Robert counts them off as though taking inventory might make the damn thing easier to deal with.

Once upon a time, Robert was scraping by as a hired bassist in Hollywood, selling other people’s demos on the street, when a bandmate who put great stock in lucky numbers told him to “cheer up.” “It was degrading,” Robert says of those days. “But, we had to eat. Super dark times.”

“I decided that day to never play for someone else’s dream again,” Robert recalls. “I started recording my own music. I learned the hard way that no one tells your story for you. My bandmates actually did support me in my breakaway dream and ended up helping me tremendously with making my first singles and videos. But, I learned it’s really all on you to make it happen and rightfully so.”

That faith in lucky numbers has a sour afterlife in the refrain, where Robert sings, “Luck won’t change your number.” The track opens in a clatter, with bright flecks of guitar sticking out of the noise. Once the drums snap into time, the guitar winds through the sort of uneasy melody The Comsat Angels used to make sound inevitable, while the bassline lays down a gothic rock groove. A little over a minute in, Ruby Mai’s saxophone takes over from Robert’s low recitation. He comes back with his voice raised, then lets it sink in again, deeper, as he draws out his ode to the “queen of sorrow.” A rubbery bass break gives way to another round of counting before the guitar takes the song out.

Director Ilija Gavrilenko and editor Jean De Oliveira keep returning to the band under blue light, with black wisps spreading across the frame. Between those shots, a skull-faced figure in a wide black hat rides a lime-green scooter and lopes around a courtyard carpeted with fallen leaves. It looks like somebody sent a horror-movie ghoul out to run an errand.

Seattle Dungeon Synthpop Project PROFIT PRISON Asks What the Living Owe the Dead in Video for “In Memoriam”
There’s something profoundly rotten about a world where people can disappear, families can be destroyed, and the surviving witnesses are expected to carry on buying groceries and paying…
Though they’d lost control of the outskirts of their town
and I loathe to tell you how it ends
so in silence we bow our heads

There’s something profoundly rotten about a world where people can disappear, families can be destroyed, and the surviving witnesses are expected to carry on buying groceries and paying their miserable bills while history quietly buries the evidence. Human civilization has developed an extraordinary talent for committing atrocities, commemorating the dead, and finding fresh excuses to repeat the process. Somewhere in this grand procession of moral bankruptcy, Seattle’s Profit Prison has found sufficient inspiration to write a disco song about the unbearable weight of collective guilt.

The solo project of Parker Lautensleger, whose musical history includes Anteinferno, Bhereg, Victims Panel, and Excarnated Entity, has spent nearly a decade exploring the more psychologically disturbed possibilities of electronic pop. His latest single, In Memoriam, taken from the forthcoming album Why art thou wroth? And why is thy countenance fallen? , sounds like Bronski Beat wandering into a particularly unpleasant historical reckoning, with electronic pioneer Gershon Kingsley conducting the proceedings from behind an enormous bank of synthesizers.

The arrangement possesses a strange, almost indecent sweetness. Synthesizers trace delicate melodic figures above a measured electronic rhythm, their crystalline repetitions creating the impression of a forgotten European dance record rescued from somebody’s flooded basement. Lautensleger sings with a trembling, distant resignation, his voice occupying the uncomfortable space between Neil Young’s wounded sincerity and the exquisite emotional distress of early synthpop by Das Kabinette, Depeche Mode, and others you might find on the Some Bizzare Compilation. Every syllable seems burdened by information its owner would dearly prefer to forget.

And what dreadful information it is. The lyrics describe a family whose apparently stable existence has been overturned by events unfolding near a border, where some unspecified act of violence has left questions that nobody seems willing to answer. Children inherit uncertainty, the dead receive their solemn acknowledgments, and the living are forced to contemplate the possibility that their own moral identities have been built upon carefully maintained ignorance. The song’s repeated interrogations grow increasingly desperate, suggesting a confrontation with somebody whose participation in an atrocity has become impossible to dismiss. Beneath the delicate electronic flourishes lies the hideous proposition that ordinary people can commit extraordinary acts of cruelty and subsequently spend entire lifetimes inventing explanations for themselves.

In Memoriam ‘s synthesizers maintain their patient, hypnotic progression while the words wander into the ugliest corners of human responsibility. You could conceivably dance to this record, which raises some rather uncomfortable questions about the emotional usefulness of disco. Lautensleger leaves those questions unanswered, however, allowing the music to continue its beautiful, merciless rotations while the accumulated weight of memory threatens to crush everything beneath it.

The video takes on a philosophical matter, as though we’re prisoners in Plato’s cave, watching distorted projections of events whose true nature remains somewhere beyond our comprehension. The road stretches onward, the lights assault our vision, and every image seems to conceal a fragment of some dreadful revelation.

The very British problem of GB Music Radio
GB News has launched an all-British radio station. As nationalistic thinkers so often do, they've oversimplified what it means to be British, and diluted the quality of their output in the…

How do you find common ground between a Guardian reader and a Daily Mail reader? Get them talking about British music. Somewhere down the line, they’ll share some musical common ground, or at least bond over their reverence – despite said reverence likely coming from different places – of the factory of musical greatness that is this strange little island.

For the right wing, perhaps it’s a beacon of what makes Great Britain greater than anywhere else. For the left, our music and culture might be the one thing about this country they can feel proud of in an era of decaying support structures and rampant division.

There’s something ironic, then, about right-wing slop spewers GB News positioning their new all-British radio station as a source of unity. Upon its announcement last month, Chief Revenue Officer Ross Sergeant said: “GB Music Radio gives advertisers something genuinely new: a station built around a single, warm idea that almost everyone in this country can get behind.”

Music should be the great unifier. Can a radio station really do that, though, when it’s had red, white and blue vomited all over it courtesy of arguably the most polarising, untrustworthy and hateful news brand in the country? It’s doubtful. For that reason alone, plenty of people wouldn’t touch it with a bargepole.

In fact, something about its announcement felt ridiculous enough to be satirical, especially with how it positioned its show names, like ‘Great British Drive Home’ and ‘Great British Breakfast’. So this is a station for people who chant ‘Come on Ingerland’ as they wolf down their bacon sarnies in the morning before sitting in their very Bri’ish traffic jam (in a vehicle that is decidedly not British)?

Sergeant added: “British music is a shared passion that cuts across generations, and we look forward to helping brands become part of the soundtrack to our listeners' day, from Breakfast with Paul [Coyte] to weekend mornings with Nana [Akua].” Coyte and Akua are already established names on GB News, the former presenting sports shows before pivoting back to music, while Akua recently went viral for a heated exchange with a guest on a panel last month.

Consequently, 'All British, all day’ once again spits in the face of any sort of unity. There’s no hiding the nationalism behind it, as it turns music into a cultural battleground it has dominance over, wresting it out of progressive hands into something it can call its own.

The arts and culture sectors, particularly music, are overwhelmingly left-wing , and music has for decades been a site of community building and changemaking, from Seventies punk values to recent calls for boycotts and solidarity with Palestine.
More recently, when the right have wanted a piece of this, they’ve even turned to AI-generated figureheads such as Danny Bones, who we investigated on the podcast.

GB Music Radio’s other problem is it tries to make the idea of Britishness far more simple and far less nuanced than it is in reality. Who gets to be considered British? What about mixed-nationality artists? Does AI count?

A spokesperson tells Drowned in Sound: “We celebrate British music in the broadest possible sense. British artists, or groups who are British or have British members. For example we will feature Fleetwood Mac. GB Music already features AI generated content in our hourly traffic AI reports but there are no plans for any fully AI songs."

It’s better that it’s broad, of course. To strip away all but the most ‘purely’ British artists certainly leaves the pool looking about as bland and beige as a plate of potato smileys sans sauce. Looking at what they've played at the time of writing, the playlist includes Lewis Capaldi's 'Survive', Pulp's 'Disco 2000' Kajagoogoo's 'Too Shy', Rainbow's 'Since You've Been Gone', David Bowie and Queen's 'Under Pressure' and Duffy's 'Mercy.' These are all songs you could hear if you whacked on Heart, Virgin Radio and the like. It's not all that different from a lot of middle-of-the-road mainstream radio, except without the variety an all-nationality playlist could offer.

Last Tuesday I went to Paris for my birthday. I came home yesterday, and I miss it. I miss friendliness, everything feeling slower, good vegan food, sleeping in a bed that doesn’t hurt my back and a decent shower. It was the perfect way to see off my 30s, and the last band I saw of my 30s on the day before my birthday was Penelope Isles.

What made the show special is that Lily, Jack and I are from the Isle of Man. I felt like a piece of home was in the room on Wednesday night and there were times where I was trying to not cry a little. It’s weird because I have such a weird relationship with the Isle of Man, but that’s not for here. That’s for elsewhere.

I’ve only been to gigs in the UK but I can honestly say that the crowd at Supersonic were just lovely, and it was a joy to be in such a beautiful environment. People were respectful of personal space and there were no drunken idiots ruining it for everyone. Although the set was just under an hour; it was a perfect set. Every song was delivered in such a perfect and tender way. You felt every song, and connected with every word. The set opened with 3, and it was straight into Thinking Seat which just hits you right in the soul and all feels okay. For me, it was Birthdays that did it. That song very nearly got tears out of me (it’s been a comfort) and to see it live was such a gorgeous moment, and it makes you appreciate the song and the record in general, even more so when you see it live. Another Kind Of Love shows just how delicate Jack’s vocals are, and where there are moments in the set where Jack, Lily and Joe absolutely tear the roof off the venue (especially during Gnarbone, which was an insane way to end the show)- you just really see how bloody talented this band is, and they truly deserve the world.

The room felt like it was filled with love and just appreciation for the band, and maybe it was extra special because it was the last night of the tour, but it just felt like one of those shows that people will talk about in years to come and those of us who were there will know exactly how lucky we were. It was a truly stunning show, and is up there as being one of my favourites of the year. Lily, Jack and Joe are just exceptional musicians, and it was a real honour to witness their greatness last week. I also felt super proud that a band from where I’m from are playing venues like Supersonic and just being a dream to watch.

At the end of the show, my partner and I went up to the merch stand and Lily spotted my Bushy’s t-shirt. I told her I was from the Isle of Man, and it was one of the most wholesome moments I’ve had. Jack and I had our photo taken together, with our Bushy’s shirts, and spoke about home for a little bit. It was nice to have a piece of home and to meet the band who have again, released one of the best records of the year.

If you’ve not listened to 3 yet, I urge you to do so. There is so much love, loss, thought, care and heart on the record and when you witness it live- you hear the record differently. The bond between Jack and Lily is so beautiful, and you just feel so lucky to witness the greatness of all 3 of them on stage together. At times the songs are mellow and soothing, and there are other moments in the set where this gorgeous loudness takes over. Ending the set with Gnarbone was just heaven! Opening or closing with it was always going to be magic!

Another Kind Of Love going into Birthdays then into Moonwalker was a piece of musical heaven. I honestly couldn’t have wished for a better band to say bye bye to my 30s to (I saw Fontaines D.C the day after my birthday on Friday, so I really have lucked out here!)

What does access look like for disabled gig goers in 2026?
The average disabled music fan faces spending an extra £99 to attend a gig

Attitude is Everything connects disabled people with music and live event industries, to improve access together. Starting in 2000, the charity has supported industry pros and organisations to help better understand and improve access for Deaf, disabled and neurodivergent people in music.

The charity’s State of Access Report - a report set up to set standards for national progress with disability in music - lays out exactly what that looks like in 2026, and how fraught with problems it can be, alongside the scale of the extra burden it places on disabled fans so they can safely enjoy their night out.
It’s the first report in eight years, and the first since Covid-19. In that time, the volume of the conversation around access in live music has hit a fever pitch.
It's partly out of necessity, given that Covid-19 has been described as a "mass disabling event", and as of 2023, 2 million people in the UK are estimated to be living with long Covid.

This fan-led review echoes similar calls to improve inclusion across music events. 24% of Music Fans Voice respondents disagreed (compared to 58% who agreed) with the statement that live music events currently reflect the demographic diversity of the UK.
There's a disability tax on attending live gigs

The average disabled music fan faces spending an extra £99 to attend a gig, the most common of which (66%) relates to travel or accommodation. Other common access related costs include health or recovery costs (40%), personal assistant or companion costs (28%), higher ticket prices (25%) or food and drink for medical purposes (23%). Sadly, 58% of fans say extra costs have stopped them from attending an event.

The most frequent barrier disabled fans encounter relates to poor or inaccurate access information, which 69.5% of fans say they've experienced. Meanwhile, lack of seating or rest spaces is a barrier for 66.4% of respondents, booking or ticketing systems for 56.1% and staff attitudes or behaviour for 51.6%.
Access is inconsistent across the board

Only 20% of disabled gig goers say they feel they can consistently rely on their access needs being met. Even more starkly, 94% say they expose themselves to some level of risk when they go to a show.
The burden still falls on disabled people to advocate for themselves

72% of disabled gig goers have had to resolve access problems themselves, while 62% report having to explain their needs repeatedly. Just under half (48%) of respondents have said they've supported other disabled fans in the past, while more than half say they've had to leave events early due to access issues.
Fortunately, 58% of those surveyed said that they think access has improved in the last five years, and 61% would describe events as 'somewhat' or 'very' accessible.

"The findings from the survey are shocking, but sadly not surprising. But, by sharing the feedback with the sector, and supporting the music industry to embed access, we aim to improve the experiences for the disabled community, because by removing barriers, we don’t just open doors, we open up an entire industry."

Here’s Which Hunger Games Character You Are, According to Your Zodiac Sign
Would you volunteer as tribute—or take center stage as the main villain? Astrology has the answer to that and more.

For our first zodiac sign, we’ve got a new character in the series. In Sunrise on the Reaping , Maysilee joins a young Haymitch and two other tributes from District 12. At the start, Maysilee seems arrogant, condescending and even a little prissy—none of which are typical Aries traits. But soon it becomes clear that Maysilee is actually passionate, blunt and not afraid to start a fight. Now, that’s you, Aries!

Because you’re ruled by action-packed Mars, you’re the one who always says the thing everyone’s afraid to say and who puts revolution into motion. And that’s Maysilee to a T. She pushes against Panem’s dysfunctional structure by refusing to fall in line—mocking Capitol fashion on live TV, refusing to cry on camera and encouraging her co-tribute, Louella, to demand better silverware on the train. In the book, she tells Louella, “If you let them treat you like an animal, they will.”

Interestingly, Maysilee is the first owner of the iconic mockingjay pin that Katniss finds in the first Hunger Games movie. The image of the mockingjay itself becomes a symbol for the revolution in later movies—and it started with this young woman, who wouldn’t go down without a fight.

Katniss’s vibe matches your sign’s bull-headed attitude, Taurus. Her authenticity and grounded nature make her completely allergic to attention, spectacle and anything that feels like a performance. Taurus rules both nature and the material things we need for stability and support (like food or shelter), so it’s no wonder that Katniss is the one who hunts for her family and feels more comfortable in the woods than she does among people.

Of course, she’s also fierce, brave and bold. You might think she’d be an Aries for those reasons, but Katniss only ignites for a reason, whereas Aries doesn’t need a reason to act out. Think about it: Katniss strikes back only when slighted first, like when she jabs the knife in the table when no one responds and when she shoots the arrow at the pig when she’s ignored. Then there’s a fact that you’re a little slow to do … everything . Katniss thinks things through and takes calculated risks, and she’s slow to open up, even to Peeta.
I originally picked Taurus for Katniss simply because it makes sense (and you know it!). But lo and behold, Katniss’s birthday is, in fact, on May 8, which means she’s a full-blooded Taurus!

You’re the chatterbox of the group, Gemini, which makes sense since you’re ruled by Mercury, the planet of communication and quick wit. As a television host, Caesar is basically a professional talker, and well, did we mention that you kind of love talking? You can literally spark a conversation with anyone and get them to open up. For Caesar, that means encouraging a shy girl like Rue to share her strengths, pumping up the ego of District 1’s socialites, and tugging on the heartstrings of every viewer in the Capitol—all within a five-minute segment.

Your other special talents include sarcasm, jokes and the tactical ability to change topics seamlessly when it’s uncomfortable. Caesar is exceptional at these things, which helps him avoid plenty of national, broadcasted disasters. Remember when he cut to commercial when Peeta brilliantly announced that Katniss was pregnant?

Now, before you disagree with this one (because honestly, I probably would have too), the new Hunger Games film actually answers this question for us. Sunrise on the Reaping follows a young Haymitch on the day that he’s chosen as a tribute—which just so happens to be his 16th birthday. Every reaping occurs on July 4, which means Haymitch is a cuddly, sweet, crabby Cancer.

And it makes sense when you think about it. Haymitch is protective, passionate, committed and sensitive. Plus, in the new movie, similar to what Katniss does with Rue, Haymitch takes 12-year-old Lou Lou under his wing, which feels incredibly maternal—your specialty! If there’s a baby bird out there in need of help, you’re the first one on it.

Hey folks. Like the rest of the internet & other tech infrastructure, KDO has seen some outages in the past week or so, amounting to a few hours of downtime. Our time here together isn’t what I would call mission critical — reading the site an hour or two after you’d originally wanted to is not the worst thing in the world — but it’s still a bummer to have the site be unavailable.

The reasons for the KDO downtime have been various, but that it occurred around the same time as some of these other outages isn’t, IMO, coincidental. Security researchers and developers armed with LLMs are going bananas finding exploits in a bunch of the software and infrastructure underpinning, well, everything. On the other side of the aisle, sysadmins are scrambling to fix all of these newly found exploits.

But of course, poking holes in things is easier & faster than plugging them. LLMs can help with the patching, 1 but it’s asymmetric warfare — being slow & careful with upgrades and patches isn’t a luxury you have when so many things are coming at you on a daily basis. Hopefully the situation won’t get too much worse before it gets better, but in the meantime, I’m thankful for everyone who is trying to keep these systems running. 🙏

Second thing: after a few months on the other side of the world, I’m spending some time with my family for Thanksgiving, and so the site will be a bit slower this week and very early next week. I’ve been pushing quite a bit over the past several weeks and it’s nice to take a bit of a break.

Is It Really Rude to Ask Who Else Is Coming Before You RSVP?
I'm happy to attend your party. I'm just wondering if I'll know anyone there. Is that so wrong? Here are the etiquette rules. The post Is It Really Rude to Ask Who Else Is Coming Before You…

An extended family member once made an accidental enemy of my 3-year-old son by giving him clothes for his birthday. Like many little kids, he was a nudist at heart and didn’t consider clothes a gift so much as a punishment. (This child used to call pants “leg jails.”) So when we showed up to the family party later that year, he took one look at said relative and announced at the top of his lungs: “NOT YOU AGAIN—I HATE THIS PARTY.” Clearly, it would have been useful for him to know the guest list in advance (if he could read, which he couldn’t). But he was just saying out loud what many adults have found themselves thinking in various social situations.

Take, for example, a friend of mine who throws a massive holiday party every year. It’s a Kardashian-level event, if the Kardashians lived in suburbia and wore Anthropologie. We’re talking well over 100 invitees. The guest list probably needs its own zip code. I usually know maybe 20 of them. Thankfully, though, she sends the invite through Facebook, which means I can see exactly who has RSVP’d. I’m not proud of this, but I check it. Repeatedly. Like a day trader watching a stock. If a good chunk of my people are on the “Going” list, I’m in, and I will even put on real pants. If it’s a sea of strangers and one lady I once nodded at in a parking lot, I suddenly remember I might have a thing that night.

Does the guest list influence my decision? Absolutely. Do I feel guilty about it? Also absolutely. I should want to go for the hostess, shouldn’t I? She’s wonderful. Her party is wonderful. Supporting my friend should be reason enough. Instead, I’m evaluating her guest list like a Google review page.

But before you judge me, admit it: You do this too. Everybody does this. Nobody commits to a party completely blind, and anyone who claims otherwise is either lying or has better self-esteem than I do. The real etiquette question is what to do when the guest list isn’t conveniently posted on the invite. Is it rude to just ask the host, straight up, “So who else is coming?” I have thought about this far more than a grown woman should. Here’s where I landed.
The case for asking the host

Everyone wants to know who’s coming. It’s just human nature. The only difference is whether you ask or quietly stalk the RSVP list like it’s an ex’s Instagram. Asking the host is just the honest version of what we’re all doing anyway.

Going to a party takes real effort: the clothes, the sitter, the drive, the small talk, the dessert you bring that you put on a fancy plate hoping no one will notice you got it from the grocery store . Wanting to know whether you’ll see a friendly face at the party isn’t snobbery—it’s basic risk assessment, and the host is the one person who has the answer.
And sometimes, it’s about more than whether the company is fun. I don’t know about you, but if an ex or an ex-friend might be there, I’d at least like a little warning before I walk in.
The case against asking the host

This question is so awkward. How do you even start that conversation? A party isn’t a menu, and your friend isn’t a waiter. Asking who else is coming can sound like you’re ranking their party, and the host might hear, “I’ll only show up if the cool people do.” Nobody wants to feel like their party is the backup plan.
It can also put the host on the spot. She invited you because she likes you, and now she’s reciting names like a court bailiff while wondering if she’s passing some kind of friendship test.

But the biggest issue is that you risk making the host feel unimportant to you, or at least less important than those other people. Because you are literally telling her that she’s not reason enough for you to attend. Ouch.
The real problem isn’t the question

Yet, as awkward as it feels, asking who’s coming isn’t the rude part. What you do next is. The rude part is the limbo where you check “maybe” (or nothing at all) on the RSVP list and let days or weeks go by while waiting to see who else is coming. Meanwhile, your host is just trying to figure out the head count she needs for food, chairs and her own sanity. Hosts aren’t mind readers, and “I’ll let you know” without ever letting them know is so rude.
